1:
How the opening clauses divide is Calvin’s first question. Some join the words to me with the first clause, so that it runs, if thou returnest, Israel, to me, and read separately, thou shalt rest; others render, if thou wilt return, Israel, return to me. Calvin thinks the most suitable rendering is, if thou wilt return, Israel, rest in me, and wholly rejects as forced the version, if thou wilt return to me, Israel, thou shalt rest. The substance is the same either way, since the prophet is condemning a hypocrisy that had often professed readiness to obey and proved the profession false; and on the second reading the intimation is that they took circuitous courses so as not to return directly, it being usual with hypocrites to make a great show of repentance while shunning God.

Henry hears the verse as a reply to something just said. The people had answered the call by saying, Lord, we return, and God takes notice of it: dost thou say, I will return? Then return unto me and make thorough work of it, not only turning from idolatry but returning to the instituted worship, and doing it rather than talking of it. The abominations are to be put away out of the sight of God, out of all places, since every place is under his eye; and sin must be put away out of the heart, or it is not put away out of his sight at all. Ellicott glosses the word as things of shame, the idols Israel had worshipped, and takes the closing clause not as a promise but as one more condition, if thou wilt not wander. Clarke reads it as promise: this was spoken before the captivity, and even that threatened judgment would have been averted by returning.

The swearing they all take as a part standing for the whole. Gill says it means by the living Lord, by him only, not by the creatures but by the God of truth, and that it is sometimes put for the whole worship of God. Calvin turns it against them: having the name of God in their mouths they thought themselves absolved from all guilt, boasting that they were the seed of Abraham and treating an external profession as an expiation, whereas they were sacrilegious in professing that name falsely. Clarke puts it as a charge, to bind themselves by God and to God and by no false god.

Henry draws three rules out of the three words that follow. We must swear by the true God only; we must swear only what is true, not daring to assert what we do not know to be true nor to promise what we do not mean to perform; and we must do it solemnly, when judicially called to it, since rash swearing profanes the name of God as much as solemn swearing honours it. Calvin takes truth here for integrity, and holds there is no worship of God without sincerity of heart; but truth is especially known by the two words after it, when men deal faithfully with one another and render to all their right.

What the nations do is read three ways. Ellicott says that if the conditions of a true repentance are fulfilled, the outlying heathen nations shall bless themselves in the Lord, owning and adoring him and being blessed by him. Clarke expects them to be so convinced by the change wrought on Israel that their usual form of benediction will become, May the God of Israel bless thee. Calvin finds an indirect reproof in the clause, since the name of God had been exposed to heathen who said there was no power in him to help, while the people expostulated with God as though they had just cause of complaint, having been promised that they should be models of his blessing.
3:
The address changes hands here, and they all notice it. Keil and Delitzsch treat the exhortation to reform as the ground of the exhortation to return that went before, the earlier condition having been the indirect call to repent addressed to Israel, the call now coming to Judah. Ellicott says the words seem at once the close of one discourse and the opening of another, the parable of Israel being left behind and the appeal made more direct; the phrase, he notes, is literally to each man individually. Henry marks the difference of audience: the prophet had proclaimed comfort toward the north, to those humbled in captivity, and now speaks to men in prosperity, for their conviction.

The fallow ground they explain from husbandry. Clarke defines it as ground once tilled and long left uncultivated: they had been long uncultivated in righteousness. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew gets its force from a verb and noun of the same root, and says the spiritual field needed exposure to the sun and free air of God, to the influences of light and warmth and the dew and soft showers of his grace. Henry works the figure hardest. An unconvinced and unhumbled heart is like fallow ground, untilled and unoccupied; it is our own ground let out to us and we must account for it, but it lies unfenced and common, unfruitful, overgrown with the thorns that are the natural product of a corrupt heart. We are therefore to search our own hearts and let the word of God divide as the plough does, and to pluck up by the roots the corruptions which, as thorns, choke both our endeavours and our expectations.

Calvin turns the figure against a pretended diligence. Scripture often compares us to a field, since we are the heritage of God and he means to gather fruit from us; and hypocrites do sow, pretending great ardour when God calls them to repent, but they mar everything with their own mixtures, like a man scattering seed among thorns. It will avail nothing to cast seed there, for the ground must first be cleared; and Calvin presses the wording, that the command is literally to plough for themselves the ploughing, so that they were not to sow a land once ploughed but to plough it again, a people hardened in their vices needing an unusual cultivation. Clarke adds the same warning, that when the seed of the word of life is sown, worldly cares must not be allowed to rise and choke it; and Ellicott hears in the clause the germ of a later parable, where likewise the seed is the word of God.

The second command drops the figure only halfway. Gill says the circumcision meant is of the heart, as the following words show; Clarke, that it means putting away everything that tends to grieve the Spirit of God or render present resolutions unfruitful. Ellicott finds in the phrase proof that the prophet had grasped a symbol which to many was merely an outward sign, the foreskin of the heart being the fleshly unrenewed nature; and he traces the wording to an earlier book whose influence is felt throughout this prophet.

Calvin makes the rite itself the argument against them. Why was circumcision enjoined, if not to show that a man who aspires after true religion must begin by putting off the evil propensities of his flesh, dying to himself and to the world? They had no excuse and went not astray through ignorance, since the rite that initiated them into the service of God had taught them that he is not faithfully served except where men deny themselves. Circumcision was their great boast, but only before men, while ambition and vanity ruled in them; so they are bidden not to seek applause before the world but to consider that they have to do with God.
5:
Why the tone changes here three of them explain the same way. Gill says exhortations to repentance had been without effect in general, so that the Lord now directs the prophet to lay a view of their destruction before the people, calling on heralds to publish it through Judea and in Jerusalem. Henry puts it as a rule: the usual method of God is to warn before he wounds, and the notice must be declared in all the cities of Judah, that all might hear and fear, and by this loud alarm be either brought to repentance or left inexcusable. Ellicott says the word means to proclaim as a herald proclaims, that the cry is an alarm of war, and that the prophet sees the invading army and calls the people out of their villages into the fortified cities.

Calvin will not have it a command at all. He treats the people as irreclaimable and the words as taunting: though the trumpet is sounded after the manner of the prophets to fill them with terror, the prophet speaks by way of scorn, as if to say that when distress seizes them they will perceive that God is angry, and that though they do not believe his warnings today they will themselves sound the trumpet and cry that the enemy is at hand, let every man flee to Zion. He does not bid them sound it, on this reading, but shows what they will do; and Calvin distinguishes the passage from an earlier prophet who bade men blow a trumpet to call the people to repent.

The muster itself Henry sets out in order. The trumpet must be blown, the standard set up, a summons issued for the people to gather and draw toward Zion, either to guard it or expecting to be guarded by it; there must be a general rendezvous, the militia raised and the forces mustered. Those fit for service must go into the defenced cities to garrison them, while the weak, who would lessen the provisions without increasing the strength, must retire and not stay. Clarke reads the trumpet as a call to arms, that full information may be given to all parts of the land and the people assemble to defend themselves.

Gill will not allow the standard that meaning. It is set up, he says, not on the tower of Zion, as one interpreter holds, but on some high place pointing toward Zion, to direct the country people where to flee; and it is raised not to enlist soldiers but as a sign of danger. Ellicott reads it the same way, as a signal pointing to Zion for refuge from the foe by whom the rest of the country is laid waste.

The two words that follow are read two ways. Ellicott takes the first in a transitive sense, gather with a view to removing, and the second as linger not, the call to retreat being urgent. Calvin allows the phrase may mean either stand not, that is, hasten quickly, as men do in extreme fear, or ye shall not stand, that is, though you seek a firm position on the mount you will not continue there; the first seems to him better, as more suitable to the context. He sets the passage out as verse, calling it a spirited address in a style truly poetical.

Where the evil comes from closes the verse. Ellicott renders the clause literally, I am bringing, and takes the north for the invasion named at the outset of the book. Keil and Delitzsch set the reason of the wrath further back: the anger of the Lord has not turned away, as in blind self-delusion the people imagine, but burns on account of sins with which the prophets had long threatened them. Henry says only that it is an evil beyond all that had yet come upon the nation.
7:
Whom the lion is they all answer alike. Gill names Nebuchadnezzar out of Babylon, compared to a lion for his strength, fierceness and cruelty; Clarke names the same king and explains the second title as the destroyer of the nations, of all the people who resisted his authority, since he destroyed them all. Ellicott observes that the lion is elsewhere the symbol of a great monarchy, and that the winged lions found in the ruined palaces of the east gave a special character to what was in any case a natural metaphor; he notes too that the word rendered Gentiles answers the sense but has no particular reason to stand here rather than nations, and that the phrase about his way is literally that he has broken up his encampment and started on his march. Calvin draws the argument out of the two names: by the similitude of a lion the prophet means the people would not be able to resist him, and by calling him the desolator of nations he intimates that they would perish with the rest, for if he was able to destroy many nations, how should the Jews escape?

Calvin makes much of the tense. The prophet uses the past throughout in order to show the certainty of the prediction, and so to shake with fear men who had grown torpid in their hypocrisy; for as long as God spared them they despised his judgment and promised themselves impunity in their sins. He therefore sets the matter before them as though the invader had already come with a strong and powerful army to lay Judea waste. On the word rendered thicket Calvin says it means an entangled density, as when trees are entwined together, and he finds the similitude most suitable, because the Jews never thought the king of Babylon would come out of places so remote, the passage being difficult and the expedition attended with great toil; yet the prophet says the lion would come out of his recesses, and that nothing would hinder him from breaking out into the open country.

On the desolation itself Ellicott enters a qualification. The language about a land without an inhabitant, like that of an earlier prophet, was probably in some measure hyperbolical; but the depopulation caused by the invasion, he says, must have been extreme.

The mourning that follows Calvin will not let be mistaken for repentance. A more gracious doctrine follows later, he says, but here the prophet only reminds them that a most grievous mourning was at hand, seeing them to be hypocrites immersed in their own delusions and unassailable by any fear. They were greatly mistaken if they thought themselves safe while God was angry with them; for the ungodly are wont to make God subservient to themselves, as though by their perverseness they could turn his judgment aside and restrain his hand from acting. The prophet therefore says expressly that the fury of his wrath was not turned away, and warns them that they would be miserable in every way until they were reconciled to him. Gill sets the sackcloth against the same background, that the destruction threatened was so near at hand and so certain; and Ellicott notes that from the earliest times it was the outward sign of mourning, and therefore of repentance.
9:
What fails in that day is stated three ways. Gill fixes the day as the time when the invader should come into Judea and besiege Jerusalem. Ellicott takes the heart for the mind, so that judgment and wisdom give way to panic and fear. Keil and Delitzsch say the rulers will be perplexed and helpless when the wrath bursts over them, that the word rendered astonished means to be paralysed by terror, and that the prophets are named last because the next verse cites the very word by which they had seduced the people into a false security.

Calvin uses the verse to strip away a confidence. While the royal dignity still continued, though its power was much diminished, the people relied on that distinction as protection enough, so that no denunciation moved them; and the courtiers extolled their kings. Calvin allows that the word most commonly means understanding, but notes that it also means strength, firmness and courage, and thinks that sense the most suitable here. Either way the point stands: the king will be deprived of understanding, and the counsellors who lay claim to it will be found wholly foolish. He says the same of the priests, since much glory belonged to an order set over the people by God and not self-appointed, so that an opinion prevailed that they could not want wisdom. As for the prophets, Calvin holds the name is here conceded to impostors who falsely professed it, and that the true ministers of God are not meant.

The cry that follows Ellicott calls startling but eminently characteristic. The prophet had been led to utter words of desolation; but if these were true, what was he to think of the other prophets who, speaking in the name of the Lord, had promised peace? Had the Lord not apparently sanctioned them also, and if so, had he not deceived the people? Ellicott prefers this to three others: that the words are a dramatic irony representing the prophet as having shared the hopes of the people; that they contrast his predictions with the visions of an earlier prophet; and that the text should be altered to read, it is said.

Keil and Delitzsch take it for a sigh addressed to God on hearing the announcement of judgment, and note that an ancient paraphrase renders it a supplication, receive my prayer, O Lord God. They reject a proposed change of the text that would make it, so that they say, since the charge of deceiving is out of place in the mouth either of the people or of the lying prophets. Clarke follows the same paraphrase, and adds that the prophet could not reconcile the devastation with the promises already made, so that he seems to ask whether the people had not been deceived by a word of peace. Gill calls the exclamation a lamentation.

Calvin rejects the readings the others accept. Some take the passage for what the people said, since the wicked, when oppressed, cast the blame on God; others explain more loosely that the prophet indirectly expostulates with God for suffering the false prophets to flatter the people. Calvin approves neither, and takes the words for a taunt exposing the adulations by which those prophets had ruined the Jews. God rendered them their just reward in suffering them to be deceived, for the world is ever afflicted with the disease of seeking flatterers; and since these men wished their vices spared and hated their reprovers, it was his will that many impostors should assume the prophetic name. The prophet therefore does not complain but derides both the impostors and the people; and finding them deaf, he turns to God, as though to say that they were worthy of such a reward who sought flatteries and endured no correction, and might now learn they had been deceived by others rather than by him.
11:
What kind of wind is meant they settle from the desert. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as a clear wind, the scorching blast off the desert, and notes that other winds might be put to use on the threshing-floor while this made such work impossible, a fit symbol of the invader. Clarke gathers the pestilential winds and the pillars of sand collected by whirlwinds, common in the east, employed to show the effect of the invasion. Calvin notes that the word means sometimes clear and sometimes arid, the greatest dryness being on high ground, and takes it of the violent wind that disturbs the whole atmosphere where no clouds gather and no trees impede its course, which is why high and desert places are named. Keil and Delitzsch head the passage a description of the impending ruin, from which nothing can save but speedy repentance.

What the wind will not do is the point of the clause. Husbandmen winnow the corn so that the chaff may be carried off, but Calvin says this wind is not for clearing chaff: God had chastised in moderation before and played the physician healing the vices of the people, and since those corrections were without fruit his wrath now comes not to cleanse but to consume. The daughter of the people, he adds, means the people themselves.

The next wind is fuller, and to whom it comes is disputed. Gill takes it for a wind stronger than those that serve for fanning; the words about coming unto me, he says, regard neither the prophet nor the people but the Lord himself, and show that the wind is at his command and comes when he calls, all punishments for sin being from him. Ellicott renders the phrase for me, as doing my pleasure, and the wind as more tempestuous than those which serve the thresher, blowing away grain and chaff together. Calvin rejects as too strained the reading that makes the prophet speak for the people, as though the wind were to rush on themselves: God speaks here as judge, declaring a wind at hand by which he will overthrow all Judea, and showing that the invaders would not come of themselves but be sent to execute his orders. To speak judgments, he adds, is to execute the office of a judge and summon men to declare their cause; God had exercised great forbearance, but since his indulgence had only made them more ferocious he would now be their judge.

Three similitudes close the passage. Gill identifies the subject as the lion of the earlier verse, Ellicott as the destroyer of nations, with armies sweeping like storm-clouds over the land they will destroy. Calvin takes clouds, whirlwind and eagles to have one import, the quickness of the vengeance of God: clouds arise suddenly and spread over the whole heaven, so the calamity would begin suddenly, God rising unexpectedly after seeming long asleep, while the eagles show that once begun it would be easy for him to destroy all Judea in a moment. The reason for pressing the speed, he says, is that the Jews derided the threatenings, telling themselves many years would pass before the evil overtook them; profane men do the same still, thinking they gain something by putting off the day of vengeance.

Ellicott hears an older poem behind one phrase. Swifter than eagles may be a quotation from an ancient lament, and since a second phrase from it appears later in this chapter he thinks the borrowing something like a certainty, a man who wrote two sets of lamentations himself being likely to have studied earlier elegies. The woe at the end both he and Clarke give to the people: Clarke has them interrupt the prophet with the cry, and the prophet resume; Ellicott takes it for the cry of the terrified crowds of Jerusalem, with which the prophet identifies himself.
14:
The heart is named as the cause of the rest. Gill says the wickedness of their hearts is the cause of all their ruin: every part of a man is wicked, the thoughts, the mind, the will, the conscience and the affections; the heart is the womb in which all sin is conceived and the shop and forge in which it is wrought, the source of all evil thoughts, words and actions. Clarke puts it as a question: why not put away your wickedness, that you may be saved from these judgments, and how long shall your vain thoughts of safety lodge within you while you continue a rebel? Ellicott takes the words for the answer of the prophet to the cry from the city, and finds the one hope of salvation in a washing of the heart that seemed impossible earlier in the book but is now thought of as possible with God.

Calvin agrees about the inwardness, then guards the clause. By bidding them wash that they may be saved, the prophet shows there is no remedy but reconciliation with God, and none without repentance; hypocrites always seek to appease him by external rites, while he cannot be pacified unless they return from the heart, the beginning of true repentance being an inward feeling. But they reason foolishly, Calvin says, who make repentance the cause of salvation because the text runs, wash thy heart, that thou mayest be saved. The prophet is not speaking of the cause of salvation at all, but showing that men are thoughtless who expect a peaceable condition while they carry on war with God. We are not to inquire whether a sinner delivers himself out of the hand of God by his repentance; the one thing in view is that we cannot be safe unless God be reconciled to us, and that he will not be propitious unless we repent from a genuine feeling within.

Why Dan and Ephraim are named they answer from the map. Gill says a messenger was come from Dan, on the northern border, the side Babylon lay on, declaring the enemy was entering; not that this was so in fact, but it is set out prophetically to rouse the Jews to a sense of their sin and danger. Clarke says Dan is the first city in the land on the way from Babylon, and between it and Jerusalem lie the mountains of Ephraim, so these would be the first places attacked and the rumour from them would show the land invaded. Ellicott adds that the pair are chosen not as extreme limits, like the familiar phrase, but as stages in the march of the invader, and that the verbs grow in strength with the nearness, first announce, as of a distant rumour, then proclaim, as of a danger more imminent. Keil and Delitzsch say the messenger comes from each successive place toward which the foe approaches, so that alarm and calamity draw ever nearer, and it is high time to be cleansed from sin.

The word for the calamity is that word again. Ellicott notes that the affliction announced is the very word rendered vain in the phrase about vain thoughts, which is the word specially applied to the idols Israel and Judah worshipped; playing on its two aspects, the prophet makes the nothingness of destruction the penalty of the nothingness of the idol. Calvin allows that the word properly signifies iniquity but says it must be taken here for punishment, since the fruit of wickedness is misery; and whenever the prophets use it they intimate that evil is never inflicted except for just cause, its source being in the wickedness of men. He adds that no army stood ready when this was written, and that the prophet, having to do with men who derided him while God spared them, set the event before their eyes as present.
16:
Whom the proclamation addresses divides them. Gill takes the verse for the substance of the voice heard from the north, a summons calling the nations to join the king of Babylon against Jerusalem. Ellicott would render it, proclaim ye to the nations, calling them to gaze on the ruin of the city, and cry aloud that watchers, meaning the besieging armies, come from a far country and will raise the war cry against the cities of Judah; Clarke says the watchers are men sent to besiege fortified places.

Calvin canvasses three. Some render, remember ye the nations, and think the prophet sends the Jews to the heathen as unworthy that God should send them his usual teachers; others render, rehearse of the nations, that is, announce that the invaders are hastening to lay the land waste. Calvin prefers a third: seeing that he spent his labour in vain on a stupid people, the prophet turns away from them, so that the sense is, declare it to the Gentiles concerning Jerusalem, and let the Jews hear no more of their ruin while the vengeance of God is made known to the heathen.

The keepers of a field they describe from the country. Gill takes them for men set to watch a field of corn on every side, that thieves and wild beasts may not waste it, and says the besiegers so surrounded Jerusalem that none could escape. Clarke fills in the practice: in the east grain is often sown in the open, and when nearly ripe guards are placed at intervals to preserve it from plunder; the city was watched like one of these fields, so that none could enter to give assistance and none who wished to escape were allowed out. Ellicott notes that field here has the sense it has in all early English, of open and not enclosed country, and takes the image from a tribe encamped in the open, or men watching flocks or crops; so shall the tents of the invaders be round the city, observing it, that is, blockading it. Calvin presses the same point: it is a sad thing when men flee away naked as from a fire and live in want among strangers, but the punishment prepared was so grievous that they could not save themselves even by that, God closing every avenue against them.

Why it should be so the next clause states. Calvin says the reason is added that the Jews might know these calamities came from the hand of God: he dealt not cruelly with them, nor were they visited by chance, but suffered justly; it would have availed them little to dread an approaching evil unless they acknowledged that he was punishing them for their perverseness. Calvin notes that some versions render the clause, thou hast neglected me, which he calls very wide of the original, the true reading being that she has rebelled.

The last verse leaves no one to blame. Gill lists the way they walked in and the actions they committed, their idolatries, backslidings and rebellions, as the cause of the siege, so that they had none to blame but themselves. Calvin says there is no reason to accuse God or their adverse fortune, as they and the heathen are wont to do, since their own deeds procured these things; God performs the office of a judge, and whatever happens is to be ascribed to their own wickedness. On the bitterness he anticipates their evasions: hypocrites cast the blame on God or complain of fortune, but however bitter the visitation, and though it pierce to their very hearts, they were themselves the authors of it. Ellicott would render the phrase, this is thy evil, and observes that the Hebrew word, like the English one, covers both guilt and punishment, so that she reaps the fruit of her own doing, which gives her sorrows a fresh bitterness.
19:
Whose cry this is they answer two ways. Gill allows it may be the words of the people, whose heart the calamity had reached, but thinks it rather the prophet, who either from sympathy speaks so or puts on mourning to awaken his people, the repetition being after the manner of men in pain. Ellicott allows the same two and prefers the people, since that gives more vividness and leaves the utterances of three great actors in turn, the people here, God next, and the prophet after. Henry takes it of the prophet: he cries out like a man on the rack, or as a woman in travail, and yet is well and in health and nothing ails him. A good man in such a bad world, Henry says, cannot but be a man of sorrows; and he grieves not for himself or any affliction in his family, but purely on the public account.

The physical detail two of them dwell on. Clarke traces the order: at the sight of misery the bowels are first affected, pain is next felt about the heart, and then a gush of tears with wailing is the issue; here is nature, he says, and fact also. Ellicott notes that the Hebrews took the bowels for the seat of the strongest emotions, and renders the clause, I writhe in pain, the walls of my heart, my heart moans for me.

Calvin doubts there is grief here at all. He grants that the prophets, severe as they were in denouncing vengeance, did not put off the feelings of humanity and often bewailed the evils they predicted, their courage not preventing them from sorrowing over their flesh. But here he thinks the prophet does not mourn the calamities so much as employ figurative terms to awaken a stupor, seeing the people torpid and neither fearing God nor touched with shame; the same laments are made elsewhere over Babylon and other enemies, where no real grief was felt.

The next verse announces a series without end. Gill reads it breach upon breach: as soon as one affliction is over another comes on, so that troubles come thick and fast until the destruction is utter. Keil and Delitzsch reject a loose translation that makes it wound meeting wound, since the word means not a wound but the fracture of a limb, and the verb cannot bear the sense of meeting alongside it; tidings are brought of one catastrophe after another, the devastation falling suddenly on the dwellings of those who lament. Ellicott renders it crash upon crash is reported, and notes that tent dwelling kept its place even amid the cities, so the curtains are those of the tent; Clarke says the solitary dwellings in the open country do not escape.

Calvin makes the heaping the point. God would pile evil on evil, so that they hope in vain for relief, the end of one being the beginning of another; and what especially distresses miserable men is to think their evils will last long. They imagined God would be satisfied with a trouble soon over, and at the first alleviation would have thought they had suffered enough and derided him as men escaped out of his hands. By saying the calamities were summoned, the prophet reminds them that God sits on his tribunal and adds heavier punishment to lighter when he finds the wickedness incurable; and the whole is related as past because it was seen in vision. The last verse repeats it: they are deceived if they think the enemy will march through the land a short time and go home, for the trumpet will keep sounding and the standard be displayed every day. Ellicott says the prophet sees no end to the miseries of the war, and Gill takes the standard for the signal of watchmen on the hills or the colours of the invading army.
22:
Whose words these are Gill and Ellicott agree on. Gill says it is the answer of the Lord to the prophet, giving the reason why so sore a destruction came upon them and so reconciling his providence: a people chosen above all others, and professing themselves his, had acted a foolish part in backsliding, revolting from his ways and worship, and committing gross idolatries. A people may be a professing people and yet a foolish one, Gill adds, since there are foolish professors who take up a profession without any experience of the grace of God. Ellicott says the same shortly, that God answers the question of the prophet, and that the misery comes to punish the folly and sottishness of the people and shall last as long as they last, or till it has done its work of chastisement.

Calvin makes the name itself the reproach. God calls them his people not by way of honour but to double their shame, since nothing could be more disgraceful than that a people chosen for his peculiar inheritance should be thus demented; he had chosen the seed of Abraham that they might be as lamps, carrying the light of salvation through the world. It is a monstrous thing, to be regarded with abhorrence, that his own people should be foolish: can it be, Calvin has him ask, that a people I chose for myself, with whom I deposited the covenant of eternal salvation, and whom I instructed by my word, should so madly ruin themselves?

The cause of the folly is named in the next clause, and Calvin draws two things from it. First, the kind of madness meant, since the knowledge of God is true wisdom, so that we are wise only when we fear him and senseless whenever we regard him not. Secondly, that no excuse of ignorance or mistake was allowed them, since God had made himself so familiarly known that they had no occasion to ask who should ascend into heaven or descend into the deep; the word was already set before them.

The vision that follows Gill limits in extent. The earth here means the land of Judea and not the whole world, and the words are not those of God continued but of the prophet, who describes the destruction either in spirit, or in prophecy, or in a visionary way. Ellicott finds in them words of terrible grandeur, the prophet speaking as though he had already seen the destruction consummated, and, by repeating the words I beheld as if he had passed through four distinct visions, describing its completeness. Both he and Clarke recognise the phrase that follows as the very one used in the account of the creation for the formless state of the chaotic mass before God brought it into order, so that the goodly land was thrown back, as it were, into chaos, before the words Let there be light had ordered it.

Calvin defends the repetition and then quarrels with the rendering. The prophet enlarges in highly metaphorical language on the terror of the vengeance of God in order to rouse a stupid and careless people, and the fourfold saying is not in vain: it is as though he turned his eyes to four different quarters and said that wherever he looked there appeared dreadful tokens of wrath. Men would receive all threatenings heedlessly unless they were violently roused, and this is the course the prophets especially pursued with hypocrites who were moved by no apprehension of punishment. On the two words themselves Calvin allows that some take them as synonymous, but notes that the first occurs about twenty times and chiefly conveys the idea of emptiness, being most commonly rendered vain or in vain; he calls the familiar version without form improper, since applied to the earth the word imports a land unfurnished with either produce or inhabitants.
24:
Why the mountains are named Calvin thinks evident. A greater stability seems to belong to them than to level ground, since they are for the most part stony and have their roots most firmly fixed in rocks, so that were the whole world thrown into confusion they seem so firmly based that no commotion could touch them; and yet the prophet says they trembled. Calvin will not have the second verb rendered destroyed, and does not know on what ground it is so taken, since the prophet is plainly confirming the same thing by another phrase: as he said the mountains trembled, so he adds that the hills shook, which is the proper meaning of the word. Gill says they trembled at the presence of God and at the tokens of his displeasure; Ellicott supposes that a great earthquake in the days of an earlier king, of which traces remain in another prophet, had made imagery of this kind familiar; and Clarke alone reads the mountains and hills as princes and rulers, astonished and fled.

The third look finds solitude. Gill takes it of a land left without inhabitants, the people either killed with the sword, or carried captive to Babylon, or fled into Egypt and other countries. Clarke says the land was so desolate that even the fowls could not find meat and so removed to another region, and calls the description powerfully energetic. Ellicott says that to chaos and darkness and the earthquake was now added the horrible sense of solitude, and that not man only but the creatures least open to the attacks of man were fled. Calvin explains why the loss is so great: the principal ornament of the world consists of men and living creatures, for why was the earth made so productive, bearing fruits so many and so various, except for their sake? Though it looks beautiful for its trees and herbs and fruit, its chief ornaments are its inhabitants; and by naming the birds the prophet takes a part for the whole and includes every earthly animal, saying that the earth was emptied.

The fourth look falls on the best of the land. Gill renders the phrase as a proper name, so that Carmel was a wilderness, that part of the country having been very fertile and abounding in pastures and fruit trees, though he allows the word may stand for the whole land. Ellicott calls it the vine-land become as the wilderness, and thinks the Hebrew article points to the well-known desert of the wanderings; the words about the presence of the Lord he renders literally, from before Jehovah, from before the heat of his anger, noting that the original has the emphasis of a repeated preposition. Calvin argues for the place rather than the quality: the word does mean any rich and fruitful spot, but he is inclined to take the mountain itself, because the next clause speaks of its cities being demolished, which fits a particular region better than fruitful country in general. He sets the verse against another prophet, who, speaking of the renovation of the Church, says the desert shall be as Carmel, where this one, speaking of a curse, says Carmel shall be as the desert. On the word for fierce anger Calvin adds that such language is not without its use, since men will sleep and never perceive the judgment of God unless he terrifies them as it were by thunder, and all threatenings otherwise become useless to them.
27:
The limiting clause most read as mercy. Gill treats the verse as an explanation of the vision just seen. Keil and Delitzsch say the land shall become a waste, but the wasting shall not be a thorough annihilation, nor such a destruction as befell Sodom and Gomorrah; the limitation rests on the promise that the Lord will punish Israel severely and yet not break his covenant, and all the prophets accordingly declare that after the judgments a remnant shall be left, from which a new holy race shall spring. Ellicott hears the thought echoed from earlier prophets and repeated later in this book: there was hope in the distance, the destruction was not final, the penalty was discipline. Wesley says it in a line: in the midst of judgment he will remember mercy.

Calvin will not take it so. He knows the reading that makes the clause a mitigation to relieve the faithful, lest they wholly despond, and grants that the threatening alone might fill a hundred worlds with terror, so that such relief is often added elsewhere. He notes that the word sometimes means perfection but in most places consummation, the verb signifying both to perfect and to consume, since what is consumed is perfected in the sense of coming to an end. Calvin allows that the first exposition contains a richer truth, and that all the early versions favour it, yet prefers to take the word for an end, as though God would use no moderation in his vengeance.

Who mourns comes next. Gill says the earth may be said to mourn when its inhabitants do, or when it is left uncultivated and uninhabited. Calvin refuses that: those who explain the mourning of the inhabitants diminish the force of it, for the prophet ascribes terror and sorrow to the very elements, which is far more striking than saying all men would grieve; and the clause about the heavens proves he means the land itself, which, though without reason, seems to dread the vengeance of God. By this he upbraids men with their insensibility: though they remain stupid, heaven and earth shall feel how dreadful the judgment is. Wesley says the elements are made to personate mourners, and Ellicott that, as with all true poets, nature seems to the prophet to sympathise with human suffering.

The clause about speaking Calvin takes as a claim of authorship. Some supply a word between the two verbs, because I have spoken what I have purposed, but the concise phrase will serve: God has pronounced a sentence firm and unchangeable, declaring once for all by his servants what he will do. The prophets were the heralds of his vengeance, and as their doctrine was despised then, so the world rejects it still; God is therefore introduced saying that his servants had been despised, but said nothing except what he commanded, and that he is the author of the sentence by which the people ought to have been moved.

Where the fugitives go closes the passage. Gill says not Jerusalem only is meant but every city. Ellicott calls the horsemen and bowmen a characteristic picture of the armies of the east, and notes that the words for thickets and rocks are both Aramaic, the first, elsewhere rendered clouds, being used of the dark coverts where men sought shelter; he cites the caves of the country as refuges in war. Calvin makes the sound itself the point, set against wounds: they had swelled with pride, and the prophet ridicules a confidence so inebriating that they did not dread the judgment of God; the mere sound of the enemy will frighten them, and the cities, left by their inhabitants, will fall easily, since walls do not defend themselves. The climbing he connects with the flight rather than the pursuers, so that to ascend into the clouds would not be too arduous for men so anxious.
30:
The opening words address a ruined woman. Gill reads them, O thou spoiled and undone creature, how wilt thou help thyself? which suggests that her ruin was inevitable and that she could be recovered neither by herself nor by any other. Ellicott says the sentence is clearer without the words supplied in italics: thou spoiled one, what dost thou work, that thou clothest, that thou deckest, that thou rentest? in vain dost thou beautify thyself. Calvin calls it the language of derision, by which the prophet casts down a pride gone untamed: in vain do they flatter themselves and promise aid from this quarter and that, their condition being past remedy. He reports a difficulty in the words, the pronoun of the received text being feminine while the participle is masculine, so that one scholar takes the second word for an infinitive used as a noun, giving the version, and against spoiling what wilt thou do.

The painting of the face both Clarke and Ellicott explain from the practice. Clarke takes it of the custom of introducing antimony between the eye and the lid to produce a fine lustre, which distends the lid, and supposes some used more than the ordinary quantity, so as nearly to rend it; and though she use every means of cunning to get help from the neighbouring states, it will be in vain, the reference being to the practice of harlots to allure men. Ellicott describes the same black powder, still used in the east, laid on with a stylus drawn between the eyelashes; the daughter of Zion is a woman in her costliest attire, as a queen of the old history had been, in the vain hope of fascinating her lovers, the imagery pointing to the foreign alliances the statesmen trusted in. He notes that the crimson and gold echo the old lament he had heard behind an earlier verse.

How the clauses hang together Calvin settles against others. He takes them as continuing the sentence, and calls frigid the view that turns them into relatives, who now adornest thyself, who clothest thyself in scarlet, since the relative makes the meaning different from what it is.

The last verse changes the picture. Gill says the distress of the Jews at their destruction is compared to the sorrows of a woman in travail. Wesley notes that when Scripture would express any exquisite sorrow it does so by a woman in travail, the first child being usually the most painful, and that spreading the hands is the use of persons in great anguish; Clarke says the fear and pain are naturally greatest so, and the gesture the one nature indicates for distress. Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the reason for what went before: the attempts of Zion to secure the goodwill of the enemy are vain, for already the prophet hears her agonised cry as she stretches out her hands for help and falls exhausted under the strokes of the assassin; the verb rendered bewaileth, they add, means to breathe heavily. Ellicott sets the two pictures side by side: on the one hand Zion as the harlot in her gold and crimson, on the other the forlorn castaway, in the hour of utter helplessness, stretching out her hands to implore mercy from the men who attack her, and imploring it in vain.

Calvin explains in what sense the prophet heard it. He could not hear otherwise than other men, but speaks according to the discovery made to him of a judgment then unheeded; and he exaggerates the evil deliberately, putting anguish for voice and a first child for a woman in labour. What he means is the suddenness: as a woman may be cheerful at meat and be seized on a sudden with the pain of labour, so the Jews could not escape by a false confidence, their destruction coming unexpectedly.
